item.title: A Five-Step Path to a Low-Cost Website: Self-Hosted Server, Hugo, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, and Baidu Indexing
item.description:
This is a retrospective of a website’s full evolution from launch to stability, covering five steps: a self-hosted server, a static site generator, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, and Baidu indexing. Site identity and domain information have been removed; what is discussed is the trigger, cost, and trade-offs behind each migration. The conclusions apply directly to startups and individuals.

The conclusion first: a stable website does not need a server of your own. The only hard cost across the whole path is the annual domain fee; hosting and CDN can run on free tiers, and indexing is completed through proactive submission on the webmaster platform. Each migration in the five stages was triggered by one concrete problem: the server brought self-managed operations, hand-written pages brought maintenance cost, GitHub Pages brought mainland-China accessibility and commercial-use constraints, and Cloudflare Pages plus indexing submission closed the loop. By the end of the path, the fixed cost of the website reduces to the domain alone.

item.title: A Complete Method Chain for Outdoor-Ad Spot Selection: Anti-Existence Scheduling Predicates, Grouped Quotas, and Two-Phase Greedy Selection
item.description:
This is a retrieval-method note, scoped to selecting outdoor-advertising spots against a delivery date range. Method names and step numbers correspond to a working implementation; organization, customer, and deployment details are omitted. The subject is query semantics and execution strategy, not pricing, contracts, or scheduling rules.

The conclusion first: generic paginated queries cannot express the semantics of spot selection; what is needed is a method chain of predicates, grouping, and packet-level strategy. Three judgments up front: 1) availability is an anti-existence judgment over intervals, not a status-field filter, and it can be done entirely in database predicates without precomputing occupancy tables; 2) a group quota of 1 and a quota of N are two different execution paths, switched because window functions are incompatible with ORM tenant filters; 3) excluding spot packets must propagate at group granularity, since per-spot exclusion leaves the business gap of selling twice in the same elevator or unit.

item.title: A Metadata-Preserving Watermark Pipeline for Evidence Photos: Pre-Extraction, Orientation Awareness, Rewrite-Back, and Three-Level Fallback
item.description:
This is an image-processing pipeline note, scoped to server-side batch watermarking of field evidence photos. Method names and step numbers correspond to a working implementation; organization, customer, and deployment details are omitted. The subject is preserving metadata and orientation and keeping batches reliable, not the business rules of watermark content or delivery workflow.

The conclusion first: metadata preservation cannot be an “overall copy-back” after processing; it must be a second channel running through the entire pipeline. Three judgments up front: 1) a conventional decode-draw-encode flow outputs re-encoded pixel data, and EXIF metadata, a structure inside the JPEG APP1 marker segment, is not carried along with pixels automatically[1][3]; 2) orientation correction must happen before watermark drawing, otherwise the watermark lands on the wrong pixel orientation and copying metadata back afterward cannot fix the misplaced content; 3) in batch processing, one image aborting the whole batch costs more than one failed image, so the fallback chain must be designed for “never interrupt,” not for “throw correctly.”

item.title: Differential Sync and State Convergence for Fieldwork Tasks: Set Difference, Data-Fact Ground Truth, and Three-Way Fallbacks
item.description:
This is a task-consistency note, scoped to spot tasks and real-scene tasks in media-delivery fieldwork. Method names and step numbers correspond to a working implementation; organization, customer, and deployment details are omitted. The subject is maintaining the task set and deciding task state, not crew scheduling or performance evaluation.

The conclusion first: task state should be decided by data facts, not event order; the task set should be reconciled by set difference, not rebuilt wholesale on range changes. Three judgments up front: 1) the cost of delete-and-rebuild is not performance but losing photo associations, completion progress, and assignees attached to existing tasks — no rework for field crews is a hard constraint; 2) upload success, photo deletion, and manual marking inevitably arrive out of order, duplicated, or missing in a distributed setting, and an event-driven state machine freezes those disturbances into state; 3) once successful image count versus photo requirement is the ground truth, convergence needs no event history, and three complementary scheduled fallbacks cover every direction of deviation.

item.title: The Read Gate of Multi-Tenant Isolation: Persistence Lifecycle Callbacks and Aspect Ordering
item.description:
This is an isolation-mechanism note, scoped to ORM-based multi-tenant systems with shared schemas and shared applications. Component names and step numbers correspond to a working implementation; organization, customer, and deployment details are omitted. The subject is framework-level mechanism, not conventions such as “remember to add the tenant condition in business code.”

The conclusion first: multi-tenant isolation that relies solely on ORM query filters is incomplete, and the gap is not in how queries are written — it is the primary-key load path that never passes through the filter. The repair is not another business-layer condition but a read gate pushed down into persistence lifecycle callbacks: every entity row entering the persistence context has its tenant ownership checked once at @PostLoad, and a mismatch terminates the load. Three judgments up front: 1) if filter activation matches annotations or class names, renames and package moves silently disable isolation, so drift must be eliminated mechanically; 2) wrong aspect ordering disables the whole mechanism — filter activation requires an active transaction and persistence context; 3) the write side must trust only server-side tenant context, never a caller-supplied tenant identifier.

item.title: The MCP Tool Bus: My Questions, Trade-offs, and Boundaries
item.description: This is a thinking record, not a survey. Background: I am wiring an Agent channel into my own business system, and MCP (Model Context Protocol) is unavoidable in that decision. What I actually cared about all evening was not “what is MCP”, but three questions — why is one more protocol worth it? What does a multi-user rollout really cost? And which of the capabilities it offers should I adopt, and which should I hand back?

item.title: A Digital Worker in Production: Nodes, Accounts, and Rollback Mechanisms
item.description: This post distills a digital-worker implementation in a patent formalities-examination scenario: how an in-house AI module migrated to a Workbuddy digital worker, how the existing Octopus task platform was loosely coupled to the agent, how the “digital persona” obtained a process identity, how failures roll back to humans, and where the security boundary sits. The core conclusion is one sentence: the blocker for putting a digital worker into production is not model capability—it’s process identity.

item.title: From Text to Voice: The Carrier Upgrade of Office Information and AI's Full-Picture Understanding
item.description:
This is an exploratory essay: one observation, one chain of reasoning, the half-century of prototypes found along it, and a handful of lawsuits just filed. Citations are marked with superscripts (dashed underline marks the cited content); sources are listed in the References at the end. Verify and rebut at will.

The Conclusion First

The capability ceiling of an LLM is set by the total volume of human text — and text is only one carrier of knowledge, and no longer the newest one. In office work, AI currently consumes only the part that has been textualized: what you typed, what the systems store, what the meeting tools transcribed. The sound of work — the discussion with a colleague, the phone call, the argument in the hallway — has not entered AI’s field of view. That layer happens to be the densest in the whole picture of work: how a decision was actually formed, where the disagreement sat, and what was said but never written down.

item.title: Attribution Is Not Resolution: AI Diagnosis, Organizational Context, and a Low-Cost Bypass
item.description:
This is a retrospective of a real incident-handling process. Names, the company, the platform, and locations are all anonymized; only two numbers are kept—the number of steps in the checklist and the time to closure—because the judgments below rest on them.

The conclusion first: in the diagnosis phase of this incident, the best performer was AI—one question narrowed the candidate causes down to the right category. Human troubleshooting had reached the same conclusion months earlier, yet stopped right there once the attribution was done. What actually pushed the issue to closure were two things AI could not do: knowing what the company itself had, and going on-site to pin down the mechanism that “verification happens only at PC login.” Attribution is not resolution—the breakpoint sits between root cause and workaround, and the input to that stretch is not reasoning power but organizational context.

item.title: The Trouble with This AI Project Had Nothing to Do with AI: Concurrency, Queuing, and Three Months of Misalignment
item.description:
This is a case study of an internal AI tool project. Names, the company, and the business scenario are anonymized; only hardware specs and usage scale are kept—because every judgment in this case only becomes clear through those numbers.

The conclusion first: there was no act of God in this case; at every step, a cheaper path existed. Shallow technical judgment, an unmanaged demo boundary, and a project assigned by habit rather than skill—three layers of problems stacked up over three months and finally exploded in a single meeting. Let’s take it apart. The title is the thesis of this post: taken item by item, nothing that stalled this project was an AI problem—concurrency management is backend engineering, capacity estimation is system design, the demo boundary is project management, and the assignment convention is an organizational issue.

item.title: What AI Cannot Replace: Customer-Facing Core Business Processes and the Engine That Runs Them
item.description: This post lays out a question I have been chewing on for a while: with AI this capable, what work can it not take over? My answer keeps converging on one place: customer-facing core business processes, and the process engine that carries them. This answer is not derived from first principles — it grew out of our work rebuilding our operations system, grinding through node after node of configuration. So I present it as “what we believe,” not “what must be” — if anything is off, push back.

item.title: The Upgrade of Managed IT Services: A New Option for SMB IT in the AI Era
item.description:
This post doesn’t claim to settle anything. It lays out a question I’ve been turning over for two years: is the way SMBs buy IT about to change? My leaning is yes. This article looks at it mainly through the lens of technology development, with a quick pass at the money. Push back if I’ve got it wrong.

1. Why SMB IT Supply Is Broken

Most SMBs assemble IT like this: find someone to fix computers, hire an outsourcing firm to build business systems, and once the project ships, nobody owns it. The outsourcing problem is requirements translation — the business says “I want to know at any moment which orders might be late,” and by the time it lands in the contract it has become a few screens plus a list of feature points. Acceptance passes; the business problem may still be unsolved. Traditional MSPs only cover computers, networks, and backups — they can’t afford to keep people who understand the business, can plan, and will take responsibility. The result is a gap in the middle: someone manages the cables, nobody manages the systems, and nobody at all manages “where the money goes over the next three years.”

item.title: Enterprise AI Adoption: Organizational Context, Internal FDEs, and Scenario Gates
item.description:
This post distills the framework we developed while building enterprise AI adoption plans: a four-level evolution path, four types of enterprise context, internal FDEs, three scenario gates, a five-stage rollout, and four governance pillars. Most AI projects stall at the pilot stage because nobody owns the organization, the data, and the processes—not because of the technology.

Over the past two years, companies have bought AI in nearly identical ways: purchase a batch of seats, run a few training sessions, pick two departments to pilot, then wait for the reports. Six months later, most of them are stuck at “individuals know how to use it,” while organizational capability hasn’t moved an inch.

item.title: AI-Native Engineering: Artifact Chains, Gates, and Metrics
item.description:
This is what we learned after getting an AI-native development process running end to end: the artifact chain, the distinction between constraints and assumptions, three-valued gates, three-layer metrics, and four failure modes you will inevitably hit. Installing the tools is year one; hardening the process is the actual transformation.

Last year we rolled AI coding tools into our development team. Three months later we did a delivery review, and the numbers were ugly: plenty of tool usage, no faster delivery. The cause was not the models — it was that we treated them as “faster typewriters” while the process itself never moved an inch.

item.title: API Access and Integrity Risk Catalog
item.description:
This post distills the API governance methodology developed for the Xomaps (信朴科技) location management system: a risk catalog of 17 control measures for enterprise internal systems, designed for architecture reviews, security requirement writing, and threat modeling.

Scope: enterprise internal systems — systems where the data is a company-level asset and every user is both a user and a maintainer of that asset. This includes command channels (consolidated command layer on the write side) / multi-tenant middle platforms / open APIs (MCP, mini-program mobile clients). Purpose: a standard risk catalog for architecture reviews, security requirements, and threat modeling. Positioning: belongs to the “API Access and Integrity Risk” category, alongside Transport Security and Authentication Security.
